newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb ties to Serbia risky, Carl Bildt says.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb ties to Serbia risky, Carl Bildt says.

text.p: Bosnian Serbs run the risk of financial ruin if they maintain their links with the troubled economy of neighbouring Serbia, Western envoys said on Sunday.
Citizens of Bosnia's Serb republic still use the Yugoslav dinar, the currency of their wartime patrons in Serbia and Montenegro.

The dinar has declined from 3.7 to the German mark at the end of December to between four and almost five to the mark, varying according to differences in local demand in cities across Serbia. The official rate is 3.3 to the mark.

On Sunday at an economic policy conference in Sarajevo, Carl Bildt, the international High Representative to Bosnia, and a number of foreign experts cautioned that Bosnian Serbs should distance themselves from Serbia's economy.

"For those of you representing (the Serb republic) -- if you maintain a link to the economy of Serbia as your principle economic link, you will inevitably follow Serbia downwards through the economic valley -- the valley of despair and isolation," David Lipton, assistant secretary of the U.S. treasury, told the conference.
"With the financial situation there...Serbia will not be an engine pulling you along, it will rather be a drag," he added.

Bosnian Serb republic representatives have yet to formally agree on a draft law for a single Bosnian central bank and single currency as required by the Dayton peace accords and the International Monetary Fund.

Bosnian Serb officials, who opposed Bosnia's declaration of independence from Serbian-led Yugoslavia which touched off the 1992-95 war, have sent mixed signals about their attitude towards a single currency in recent months.

But Bildt told a news briefing that the Serb republic needed "protection" from Serbia's ailing economy. "I think Serbia is on the brink of financial disaster. We have seen the dinar losing a third of its value on the black markets -- those are the real markets -- during the last week," he said.

"It's very important to protect (the Bosnian Serb republic) from the negative financial influence of the (economic) collapse of Serbia and from the very strong inflationary influences that will come from the Serbian situation," he added.
Bildt said the Bosnian Serbs had accepted a single currency in principle but still wanted to negotiate possible regional variations in the currency notes.
Diplomats say launching a functioning central bank will be a key to the success of the peace process as it would help restore economic ties across former former front lines.
